---
title: "The Automation Paradox"
subtitle: "Who Really Gets Hurt When AI Takes Over?"
---

Most coverage of AI and jobs focuses on which occupations are at risk. This project asks
a harder question: which workers are actually unable to adapt when displacement happens?

Using automation probability scores (Frey & Osborne, 2013), BLS employment projections
through 2034, and the ILO's 2025 GenAI Exposure Index, the analysis finds that 144
occupations — nearly 24% of the matched dataset — combine high automation exposure with
wages and education too low to support any transition. Automation risk and job loss are
correlated (r = −0.41) but not the same thing. The gap between them is adaptive capacity,
and it maps almost perfectly onto existing economic inequality.

A second finding complicates the picture further: the risk map has shifted. Sectors that
2013 models flagged as near-certain automation targets score among the lowest on GenAI
exposure today. Knowledge work — writers, analysts, mathematicians — is newly in the
crosshairs.

**Data sources:**

- [Frey & Osborne (2013)](https://www.oxfordmartin.ox.ac.uk/downloads/academic/The_Future_of_Employment.pdf) — automation probability scores, 702 US occupations
- [BLS Employment Projections 2024–2034](https://www.bls.gov/emp/) — US Department of Labor
- [ILO GenAI Exposure Index](https://www.ilo.org/publications/generative-ai-and-jobs-refined-global-index-occupational-exposure) — Gmyrek et al. (2025), ILO Working Paper 140
